fixes.explanation: Perfect, baker. Paul says, "For now we can go on living, as long as you are standing firm in the Lord." (1 Thessalonians 3:8). Standing firm is like a stamp pressed straight down into the dough, with no wobble and no slide. That's the picture Paul has of them. Their steadiness in the Lord means the world to him.

The text says the opposite, friend. They were torn away "…for a short time (in person, not in heart)…" and their desire to see the Thessalonians face to face was "…even more intense." (1 Thessalonians 2:17). So the desire didn't fade. It got stronger. That's why True is the answer here.

That's the one, baker. Paul writes, "…we wanted to come to you—indeed I, Paul, tried again and again—but Satan obstructed us." (1 Thessalonians 2:18). Paul names who was in the way. He also tells us he tried again and again, so he didn't give up on wanting to come.

You got it, baker! Paul asks, "…who is our hope, our joy, our crown of boasting, if it is not you yourselves in the presence of our Lord Jesus at His coming?" (1 Thessalonians 2:19). Then he says it plain: "You are indeed our glory and our joy." (1 Thessalonians 2:20). Not a trophy, not a building. The PEOPLE.

Good thinking, friend, but Paul doesn't point to Galatia here. He says, "…who is our hope, our joy, our crown of boasting, if it is not you yourselves…" (1 Thessalonians 2:19). He's talking straight to the Thessalonians. Then he adds, "You are indeed our glory and our joy." (1 Thessalonians 2:20).

Not this time, friend. Paul does mention the churches in Judea earlier in the letter (1 Thessalonians 2:14), but here he says, "…if it is not you yourselves…" (1 Thessalonians 2:19). He's talking directly to the Thessalonians. He finishes with "You are indeed our glory and our joy." (1 Thessalonians 2:20).

Careful there, friend. Paul says, "…when we were with you, we kept warning you that we would suffer persecution; and as you know, it has come to pass." (1 Thessalonians 3:4). He warned them about suffering. Nobody promised them a free pass.

That's right, baker! Timothy returned with news of the Thessalonians "…longing to see us just as we long to see you." (1 Thessalonians 3:6). The missing goes both ways. It's like two friends who pick up the phone to call each other at the very same moment.

That's it, baker. Paul says, "Night and day we pray most earnestly that we may see you face to face and supply what is lacking in your faith." (1 Thessalonians 3:10). They want to fill in what's missing in the Thessalonians' faith. A good teacher always has more to share.

Good guess, friend, but that isn't in this letter. Paul says they pray to see the Thessalonians face to face "…and supply what is lacking in your faith." (1 Thessalonians 3:10). The prayer is about the Thessalonians' faith.

Watch the fine print, friend! Paul writes, "…may the Lord cause you to increase and overflow with love for one another and for everyone else, just as our love for you overflows…" (1 Thessalonians 3:12). He says love for one another AND for everyone else. So the circle reaches beyond fellow believers. That's a big pitcher of love.

Yes, baker, you read it closely. Paul writes, "…may the Lord cause you to increase and overflow with love for one another and for everyone else, just as our love for you overflows…" (1 Thessalonians 3:12). The love is for one another and for everyone else, so it isn't only for believers. Overflowing means it doesn't stop at the edge of the cup.
